summary: Two physicists in Germany, Gunter Nimtz and Alfons Stahlhofen of the University of Koblenz, claim they have broken the speed of light, an accomplishment Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity says is impossible and would require infinite energy. In their experiment they passed 30 cm-wavelength microwaves through prisms initially forming a 40 cm cube and, as the prisms were moved apart up to three feet, observed some photons refracted and some quantum tunnelling across the gap, with tunnelling and refracted particles allegedly reaching detectors at the same time, suggesting the tunnelling photons jumped the gap "instantaneously." Some sources say the pair misinterpreted their results, citing the Hartman Effect—which predicts tunnelling time becomes independent of barrier length and can imply unbounded tunnelling velocities—and research by Herbert G. Winful of the University of Michigan that argues unusually brief delays in tunnelling "should not be linked to a velocity since evanescent waves do not propagate," while Nimtz told New Scientist, "For the time being, this is the only violation of special relativity that I know of."
